title: Stars Between the Strings
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 40 of 40
content:
Stars came out, and Greg brought the same blanket with a new patch. The overlook where we stayed until morning had its own weather, noises, and opinion about whether I was prepared. I stood in the middle of it with the kind of courage that appears after a person has already said yes. The reflex to run had not vanished because love became possible. It had simply lost the argument for the morning.

The plan was to say what had changed without pretending the beginning was simple. Greg wrote it on a receipt, then copied it onto cleaner paper when he decided the first version looked too much like a confession. Nothing was complicated, which made it frightening. Complicated plans came with exits. This one asked us to notice what we were building while we were building it. I kept my hands busy with patched fabric, ocean darkness, and returning and tried not to count the ways a good day could become a test.

Greg arrived with one joke already spent and another held in reserve. He was good at making a room less sharp. He was also good at hiding the bruise beneath the joke if nobody asked him to stop. He took my hand, waited through silence, and asked for every road that included coming home. When he looked at me, the familiar warmth was there, along with the question he was trying not to ask: was I staying because I wanted him, or because I had grown used to being wanted?

I answered by taking an active part in the mess. I answered without shrinking the answer into a joke. It mattered to do something that could not be mistaken for passive trust. Greg made space for people so generously that they could forget he needed space too. I did not want to accept his care as an endless resource. I wanted to meet him in the middle, where a hand could be offered and still be allowed to pull back.

The complication was already there: I still wanted to leave before being left, and Greg still joked near the heart. It was not a disaster. Beach City produced problems small enough to laugh at and serious enough to reveal a person. Greg's shoulders tightened. His instinct was to fix the practical thing first, then ask whether anyone had feelings about it. I caught his wrist before he disappeared into the task. He looked down at my hand as if I had interrupted a song.

We talked about the motel card, key, glovebox note, and unfinished chord. The object was ordinary when it entered our lives, but ordinary things collected meaning when we returned to them. Greg told the story again, leaving out the version where he made himself the fool. He had been young, lonely, and brave in ways he did not know how to name. I was not interested in punishing the person he had been. I was interested in the person beside me now, still learning how to ask.

“Home is where I can begin another page.” Greg said, embarrassed by the wisdom of his own sentence.

We took a break without calling it one. Greg found something cold to drink, and I sat where I could see the work waiting for us without being swallowed by it. He told me three small stories about patched fabric, ocean darkness, and returning: one funny, one embarrassing, and one that ended with him admitting he had been scared. I answered with a truth of my own. The exchange was not dramatic enough for a song, which was exactly why it mattered. Real intimacy kept happening in the unlit spaces between declarations. I could be tired and still be wanted. Greg could be uncertain and still be someone I trusted. We did not have to turn every feeling into a performance before it counted.

I told him what I wanted next. He let me promise something without demanding forever. Greg did not rush to reassure me. He did not promise never to fail or never to need more than I could give. He promised to tell me when fear was driving. That was better. A perfect man would have been a stranger. Greg was a person with a van, a guitar, a history of running, and a stubborn desire to come home honestly.

We kissed beneath the open van doors, then lay side by side under the stars. We let the rest of the night remain ours.

The stars looked like notes waiting for us. I took his hand, and we watched the sky until dawn. The song could keep changing, and so could we.

bridge_outro: By the next festival, Starwake Pier had become a place people crossed to hear one another. Greg played a set with room for mistakes, interruptions, and a very enthusiastic audience of one when Aang arrived with a borrowed flute. Iroh brought tea; Danse replaced a loose railing; Toph complained about the tempo while tapping her foot to it. Greg smiled at me over the strings, not asking whether he would be remembered forever. I walked beside him when the lights went out and helped fold the chairs. The Lanternweald was not the only home we had. It was the one where all those separate roads had begun to recognize each other.
